segments.text: Why is Christmas on December twenty-fifth? Every year, on that day, people around the world celebrate the birth of Jesus. And every year, you may hear the same explanation. The early Christians, it is said, simply took over a Roman winter festival, a feast of the sun, or the Saturnalia. It is a tidy answer. But the oldest sources are still here, and they tell a more careful story.

segments.text: The first answer begins with the sun. In two seventy-four, the emperor Aurelian built a magnificent temple in Rome to Sol, the sun god. Perhaps, the idea goes, the church placed the birth of Christ on the sun's own festival. There is support. A note in the margin of a Syriac manuscript says that the pagans celebrated the birthday of the sun on December twenty-fifth, that Christians joined in, and so church leaders moved the feast to that day from January sixth. And in the four hundreds, Pope Leo the Great scolded Christians who climbed the steps of Saint Peter's, then turned around and bowed to the rising sun.
